title: Week 8: Security Operations Centers (SOC), IR & Active Reconnaissance (Nmap)
subject: Information Assurance and Security
description: SOC & SIEM data pipelines, alert fatigue, NIST SP 800-61 IR lifecycle, RFC 3227 order of volatility, memory vs. disk forensics, MITRE ATT&CK, threat hunting, and Nmap active reconnaissance lab.
sourceFile: BCS411L S2W8 -  Security Operations Centers (SOC).pdf, BCS411L S2W8 Active Reconnaissance & Network Scanning.pdf

questions.question: Under the modern cybersecurity 'assumption of breach,' what two primary operational metrics do security operations aim to minimize?
options: Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time to Respond (MTTR)
Return on Investment (ROI) and Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE)
Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
Time to Live (TTL) and Round-Trip Time (RTT)
questions.answer: Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time to Respond (MTTR)
questions.explanation: Because preventative controls are never impenetrable, security operations focus on minimizing MTTD and MTTR through continuous monitoring, structured incident handling, and forensic investigation.

questions.question: In the SIEM Data Pipeline Architecture, what is the correct sequence of stages from raw telemetry to automated response?
options: Log Sources -> Ingestion & Normalization Engine -> Correlation Rules & Analytics -> Alert Generation / SOAR Engine
Alert Generation -> Log Sources -> Correlation Rules & Analytics -> Ingestion & Normalization Engine
Correlation Rules & Analytics -> Log Sources -> SOAR Engine -> Ingestion & Normalization Engine
Ingestion & Normalization Engine -> SOAR Engine -> Log Sources -> Correlation Rules & Analytics
questions.answer: Log Sources -> Ingestion & Normalization Engine -> Correlation Rules & Analytics -> Alert Generation / SOAR Engine
questions.explanation: Telemetry from firewalls, EDR, identity, servers, and cloud is first ingested and normalized into a common schema, then evaluated by correlation rules to detect multi-source TTPs, and finally routed to Alert Generation / SOAR playbooks.

questions.question: Which SIEM component converts disparate log formats such as Syslog, Windows Event Logs, JSON, and CEF into a standardized data model for uniform querying?
options: Log Ingestion & Normalization
SOAR Automated Playbook Execution
Hardware Write-Blocking
Risk-Based Alerting (RBA)
questions.answer: Log Ingestion & Normalization
questions.explanation: Log Ingestion & Normalization parses heterogeneous formats (Syslog, Windows Event Logs, JSON, CEF) into a common schema so analysts can query uniformly across devices and apps.

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates a SIEM correlation rule paired with a SOAR playbook?
options: Correlating 50 failed logins across hosts followed by a successful SMB connection, then automatically isolating the host via EDR and revoking the AD token
Recording a single failed user login to local disk without forwarding it
Manually emailing a PDF report once a month after patching servers
Running a hardware write-blocker before imaging an SSD
questions.answer: Correlating 50 failed logins across hosts followed by a successful SMB connection, then automatically isolating the host via EDR and revoking the AD token
questions.explanation: Correlation rules cross-reference events across telemetry sources (detecting Lateral Movement / Brute-Force), while SOAR executes automated response playbooks such as token revocation or EDR isolation.

questions.question: What causes 'Alert Fatigue' in a Security Operations Center (SOC), and how is it mitigated?
options: High volumes of low-fidelity alerts and false positives; mitigated by tuning correlation logic, Risk-Based Alerting (RBA), and automating tier-1 triage
Insufficient disk space for backups; mitigated by adding tape drives
Too few log sources connected to the SIEM; mitigated by disabling all firewall logs
Slow CPU clock speeds on endpoints; mitigated by removing EDR agents
questions.answer: High volumes of low-fidelity alerts and false positives; mitigated by tuning correlation logic, Risk-Based Alerting (RBA), and automating tier-1 triage
questions.explanation: SOC analysts face burnout and missed true threats when flooded by low-fidelity alerts; continuous rule tuning, RBA, and tier-1 automation reduce noise.

questions.question: What are the four core phases of the NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 Incident Response Lifecycle in exact order?
options: 1. Preparation -> 2. Detection & Analysis -> 3. Containment, Eradication & Recovery -> 4. Post-Incident Activity
1. Reconnaissance -> 2. Weaponization -> 3. Exploitation -> 4. Exfiltration
1. Detection & Analysis -> 2. Preparation -> 3. Recovery -> 4. Containment
1. Identification -> 2. Preservation -> 3. Eradication -> 4. Litigation
questions.answer: 1. Preparation -> 2. Detection & Analysis -> 3. Containment, Eradication & Recovery -> 4. Post-Incident Activity
questions.explanation: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 defines four sequential phases (with a feedback loop between Detection & Analysis and Containment/Eradication/Recovery).

questions.question: Building and training a CSIRT, deploying jump boxes and forensic toolkits, and authoring ransomware playbooks take place during which NIST SP 800-61 phase?
options: Phase 1: Preparation
Phase 2: Detection & Analysis
Phase 3: Containment, Eradication & Recovery
Phase 4: Post-Incident Activity
questions.answer: Phase 1: Preparation
questions.explanation: Preparation establishes the capability to respond before an incident occurs, including CSIRT training, out-of-band communications, forensic toolkits, and IR playbooks.

questions.question: During Phase 2 (Detection & Analysis), what three factors are used to assign incident severity during Categorization & Prioritization?
options: Functional impact, information impact, and recoverability
CPU utilization, disk capacity, and fan speed
Employee tenure, salary grade, and office location
Software license cost, vendor reputation, and SLA length
questions.answer: Functional impact, information impact, and recoverability
questions.explanation: NIST SP 800-61 prioritizes incidents based on functional impact to systems, information impact (confidentiality/integrity), and effort required for recoverability.

questions.question: Within Phase 3 of the IR Lifecycle, what is the difference between Short-Term Containment and Eradication?
options: Short-Term Containment limits the blast radius immediately (e.g., isolating endpoints or blocking IPs), while Eradication removes all threat components and persistence mechanisms
Short-Term Containment deletes all backups, while Eradication formats the SIEM server
Short-Term Containment is only done after Post-Incident Activity, while Eradication happens during Preparation
Short-Term Containment restores from backup, while Eradication isolates the network
questions.answer: Short-Term Containment limits the blast radius immediately (e.g., isolating endpoints or blocking IPs), while Eradication removes all threat components and persistence mechanisms
questions.explanation: Short-term containment stops active spread (isolating hosts, disabling compromised AD accounts), long-term containment applies temporary fixes while preserving evidence, and eradication removes malware binaries, scheduled tasks, and malicious registry keys.

questions.question: Which activity belongs to Phase 4 (Post-Incident Activity / Lessons Learned) of NIST SP 800-61?
options: Conducting a formal post-mortem to document root cause, timeline, financial impact, and updating IR playbooks and security controls
Disconnecting an infected workstation from the corporate VLAN
Capturing a volatile RAM dump using WinPmem
Running an Nmap SYN scan against a newly discovered subnet
questions.answer: Conducting a formal post-mortem to document root cause, timeline, financial impact, and updating IR playbooks and security controls
questions.explanation: Lessons Learned reviews root cause, timeline, and impact to close technical or procedural gaps in playbooks, firewall rules, and controls.

questions.question: According to RFC 3227 Order of Volatility, what is the correct acquisition sequence from MOST volatile to LEAST volatile?
options: 1. CPU registers/cache -> 2. Physical RAM -> 3. Network state -> 4. Secondary storage (Disk/SSD) -> 5. Archival media/backups
1. Archival backups -> 2. Local Disk -> 3. Network state -> 4. Physical RAM -> 5. CPU registers
1. Physical RAM -> 2. Secondary storage -> 3. CPU registers -> 4. Archival backups -> 5. Network state
1. Network state -> 2. Secondary storage -> 3. CPU cache -> 4. Physical RAM -> 5. Cloud backups
questions.answer: 1. CPU registers/cache -> 2. Physical RAM -> 3. Network state -> 4. Secondary storage (Disk/SSD) -> 5. Archival media/backups
questions.explanation: RFC 3227 mandates acquiring the most ephemeral evidence first (CPU registers/cache, RAM, active network sockets/ARP cache) before persistent storage and archival backups.

questions.question: Why is capturing physical RAM prior to powering down a ransomware-infected host critical?
options: RAM preserves running processes, memory-only malware, active network connections, and plain-text passwords or encryption keys that are permanently lost on reboot
RAM stores permanent NTFS Master File Table ($MFT) backups for 10 years
Powering down automatically uploads RAM contents to VirusTotal
RAM acquisition acts as a hardware write-blocker for the SSD
questions.answer: RAM preserves running processes, memory-only malware, active network connections, and plain-text passwords or encryption keys that are permanently lost on reboot
questions.explanation: Physical memory holds volatile runtime artifacts—unencrypted malware, injected DLLs, rootkits, active sockets, and decryption keys—which vanish immediately upon power loss.

questions.question: Which toolset pairs Memory Forensics acquisition/analysis with Disk Forensics acquisition?
options: Memory: WinPmem / LiME and Volatility Framework; Disk: Hardware write-blockers, FTK Imager, and dd
Memory: Nmap and Nessus; Disk: Wireshark and Suricata
Memory: Filebeat and Kafka; Disk: Splunk and Elastic
Memory: Ghidra and IDA Pro; Disk: Burp Suite and Metasploit
questions.answer: Memory: WinPmem / LiME and Volatility Framework; Disk: Hardware write-blockers, FTK Imager, and dd
questions.explanation: WinPmem (Windows) and LiME (Linux) dump RAM for analysis in Volatility Framework, while FTK Imager, dd, and hardware write-blockers create bit-stream disk images to inspect $MFT, $LogFile, and $UsnJrnl.

questions.question: How do forensic examiners prove that a disk or memory image has not been altered by even a single bit since acquisition?
options: By computing a cryptographic hash (SHA-256) immediately upon acquisition and verifying identical hashes on all future copies alongside a Chain of Custody form
By renaming the file extension from .raw to .bak
By compressing the evidence inside a password-free ZIP file
By storing the image in a Hot Tier SIEM index without logging access
questions.answer: By computing a cryptographic hash (SHA-256) immediately upon acquisition and verifying identical hashes on all future copies alongside a Chain of Custody form
questions.explanation: A cryptographic hash (SHA-256) verifies bit-for-bit integrity (any single-bit change invalidates the evidence), while the Chain of Custody form records who handled the evidence, timestamps, locations, serial numbers, and transfer reasons.

questions.question: In the MITRE ATT&CK Matrix Hierarchy, how are Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures distinguished?
options: Tactics are the 'Why' (high-level goal, e.g., Persistence); Techniques are the 'How' (specific method, e.g., T1053 Scheduled Task); Procedures are the 'Detail' (specific tool execution, e.g., schtasks /create)
Tactics are the specific CLI commands; Techniques are the firewall ports; Procedures are the OS patches
Tactics are hardware devices; Techniques are software licenses; Procedures are HR policies
Tactics and Techniques are identical, while Procedures refer strictly to CVSS scores
questions.answer: Tactics are the 'Why' (high-level goal, e.g., Persistence); Techniques are the 'How' (specific method, e.g., T1053 Scheduled Task); Procedures are the 'Detail' (specific tool execution, e.g., schtasks /create)
questions.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK organizes adversary behavior into Tactics (adversarial goal), Techniques (method to achieve it), and Procedures (exact implementation/command used by an adversary).

questions.question: How does Proactive Threat Hunting differ from traditional SIEM alert monitoring, and why are 'Living off the Land' (LotL) binaries a common hunting focus?
options: Threat hunting is an active, hypothesis-driven search through telemetry to uncover stealthy activity like adversaries abusing legitimate PowerShell/WMI tools that bypass static alerts
Threat hunting waits passively for an antivirus pop-up before investigating
Threat hunting only scans offline archival tapes once every five years
Living off the Land refers to physically unplugging servers in a data center
questions.answer: Threat hunting is an active, hypothesis-driven search through telemetry to uncover stealthy activity like adversaries abusing legitimate PowerShell/WMI tools that bypass static alerts
questions.explanation: Unlike reactive alert monitoring, threat hunting starts with a CTI-informed hypothesis (e.g., encoded PowerShell or WMI execution without dropping executables) and searches SIEM/EDR telemetry for behavioral anomalies.

questions.question: In the Week 8 Nmap Lab, what does the command `sudo nmap -sn 192.168.56.0/24` perform?
options: An ICMP ping sweep / host discovery scan that disables port scanning to determine which targets on the subnet are online
A full 65,535-port TCP SYN stealth scan with OS detection
An automated vulnerability exploitation attack against port 445
A service version detection scan targeting only UDP port 53
questions.answer: An ICMP ping sweep / host discovery scan that disables port scanning to determine which targets on the subnet are online
questions.explanation: The `-sn` flag performs a Ping Scan (no port scan) to identify live hosts on the 192.168.56.0/24 subnet.

questions.topic: Nmap Lab: TCP SYN Scan Mechanics
questions.question: During a TCP SYN Stealth Scan (`nmap -sS`), what packet sequence occurs when Nmap probes an OPEN target port?
options: Attacker sends SYN -> Victim responds SYN-ACK -> Attacker immediately sends RST to tear down the connection before completing the handshake
Attacker sends SYN -> Victim responds SYN-ACK -> Attacker sends ACK to establish a full session
Attacker sends FIN -> Victim responds ACK -> Attacker sends HTTP GET
Attacker sends UDP -> Victim responds ICMP Port Unreachable
questions.answer: Attacker sends SYN -> Victim responds SYN-ACK -> Attacker immediately sends RST to tear down the connection before completing the handshake
questions.explanation: Because the three-way handshake is never completed (RST is sent immediately after SYN-ACK), `-sS` is faster and less likely to be logged by basic application-level logging than a full TCP Connect scan (`-sT`).

questions.topic: Nmap Lab: Stealth vs. Connect Scan
questions.question: Why is a TCP SYN Scan (`-sS`) considered 'stealthier' than a standard TCP Connect Scan (`-sT`) against basic application logging?
options: Application daemons typically log connections only after the full 3-way TCP handshake completes; `-sS` tears down with RST before completion
`-sS` encrypts all packets with AES-256 so firewalls cannot see them
`-sT` sends zero packets over the network and guesses ports offline
`-sS` spoofs the MAC address of the default gateway automatically
questions.answer: Application daemons typically log connections only after the full 3-way TCP handshake completes; `-sS` tears down with RST before completion
questions.explanation: A `-sT` scan uses the OS `connect()` syscall to complete the full 3-way handshake, triggering application logs, whereas `-sS` aborts with a `RST` after receiving `SYN-ACK`.

questions.question: By default, Nmap scans only the top 1,000 most common ports. Which command in the lab scans ALL 65,535 TCP ports at an accelerated rate of at least 1,000 packets per second?
options: sudo nmap -sS -p- --min-rate 1000 192.168.56.20
sudo nmap -O --top-ports 1000 192.168.56.20
questions.answer: sudo nmap -sS -p- --min-rate 1000 192.168.56.20
questions.explanation: `-p-` is shorthand for ports 1–65535, and `--min-rate 1000` instructs Nmap to transmit at least 1,000 packets per second.

questions.question: How does Nmap Service Version Detection (`-sV`) identify exact software names and version numbers (e.g., `vsftpd 2.3.4`, `OpenSSH 4.7p1`)?
options: It sends protocol-level queries (like HTTP GET or FTP HELO) and compares returned banners against the `nmap-service-probes` database
It logs into the target via SSH and reads `/etc/os-release`
It guesses software versions strictly from the target's IP address
It queries DNS TXT records on the local router
questions.answer: It sends protocol-level queries (like HTTP GET or FTP HELO) and compares returned banners against the `nmap-service-probes` database
questions.explanation: Nmap `-sV` probes open ports with application-layer requests and matches the responses against `nmap-service-probes`.

questions.question: How does Nmap OS Detection (`-O`) fingerprint the target operating system when service banners do not explicitly state the OS?
options: It sends TCP/UDP packets with varied header flags and options (Window Size, IP ID sequence, TCP Options order) and matches stack responses against `nmap-os-db`
It reads the Windows Registry over port 80
It checks the HTML `<title>` tag of the default web page
It relies exclusively on ICMP Echo Reply TTL being 255
questions.answer: It sends TCP/UDP packets with varied header flags and options (Window Size, IP ID sequence, TCP Options order) and matches stack responses against `nmap-os-db`
questions.explanation: Each OS TCP/IP stack has subtle implementation quirks (window sizes, IP ID generation, TCP options ordering) cataloged in Nmap's `nmap-os-db` signature file.

questions.question: What four capabilities are combined into Nmap's single `-A` (Aggressive Scan) flag?
options: OS detection (`-O`), service versioning (`-sV`), script scanning (`-sC`), and traceroute (`--traceroute`)
ARP spoofing, DHCP starvation, DNS poisoning, and password cracking
Ping sweep (`-sn`), UDP flood, MAC cloning, and firewall disable
Memory dumping, disk imaging, hash calculation, and log deletion
questions.answer: OS detection (`-O`), service versioning (`-sV`), script scanning (`-sC`), and traceroute (`--traceroute`)
questions.explanation: In Step 2.3 of the lab, `sudo nmap -A` combines OS detection, version detection, default script scanning, and traceroute.

questions.question: In what programming language are Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) scripts written, and which NSE category checks target services against known CVE patterns?
options: Written in Lua; the `vuln` category checks services against known CVE database patterns
Written in Python; the `safe` category runs destructive buffer overflows
Written in Bash; the `default` category patches vulnerable daemons
Written in C++; the `auth` category disables multi-factor authentication
questions.answer: Written in Lua; the `vuln` category checks services against known CVE database patterns
questions.explanation: NSE scripts are written in Lua. Common categories are `safe` (non-intrusive), `default` (basic enumeration), `vuln` (known CVE checks), and `auth` (authentication/default logins).

questions.question: In the lab's targeted NSE output for port 21 (`sudo nmap -p 21 --script=ftp-anon,ftp-vuln*`), what critical vulnerability was detected on `vsftpd 2.3.4`?
options: vsftpd 2.3.4 Backdoor Execution (CVE-2011-2523) triggered by the `:)` smiley face sequence, alongside Anonymous FTP login (code 230)
MS17-010 EternalBlue remote code execution over SMBv1
Heartbleed OpenSSL TLS memory disclosure
Log4Shell JNDI remote lookup injection
questions.answer: vsftpd 2.3.4 Backdoor Execution (CVE-2011-2523) triggered by the `:)` smiley face sequence, alongside Anonymous FTP login (code 230)
questions.explanation: The lab output shows `ftp-anon` (Anonymous FTP login allowed, code 230) and `vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor` (CVE-2011-2523), which opens a shell when triggered with `:)`.

questions.question: Which Nmap command from Step 3.2 checks target ports 139 and 445 for critical flaws like MS17-010 (EternalBlue) and MS08-067?
options: sudo nmap -p 139,445 --script=smb-vuln* 192.168.56.20
sudo nmap -p 80 --script=http-enum,http-title 192.168.56.20
sudo nmap -p 21 --script=ftp-anon 192.168.56.20
sudo nmap -sn --script=safe 192.168.56.0/24
questions.answer: sudo nmap -p 139,445 --script=smb-vuln* 192.168.56.20
questions.explanation: Ports 139 and 445 serve NetBIOS/SMB; `--script=smb-vuln*` audits for critical SMB vulnerabilities such as MS17-010 and MS08-067.

questions.question: What is the primary operational risk of executing the entire `--script=vuln` category against a live production business network during working hours?
options: Intrusive vulnerability probes can crash fragile legacy services, cause Denial of Service (DoS), saturate bandwidth, and trigger massive SOC alert storms
It automatically patches and reboots all domain controllers without permission
It permanently deletes the `nmap-os-db` file from Kali Linux
It converts all TCP ports into UDP ports
questions.answer: Intrusive vulnerability probes can crash fragile legacy services, cause Denial of Service (DoS), saturate bandwidth, and trigger massive SOC alert storms
questions.explanation: Running all `vuln` scripts indiscriminately sends malformed or aggressive probes that can destabilize production applications, degrade network performance, and overwhelm monitoring teams.

questions.question: How does applying the MITRE ATT&CK framework enhance an incident response team during the Containment and Eradication phase?
options: It maps observed adversary techniques (e.g., T1053 Scheduled Task) to related persistence and lateral movement methods so responders hunt and eradicate all attacker footholds, not just the initial alert
It replaces the need for backups during the Recovery phase
It encrypts the Chain of Custody form so auditors cannot read it
It guarantees zero false positives in unauthenticated Nmap scans
questions.answer: It maps observed adversary techniques (e.g., T1053 Scheduled Task) to related persistence and lateral movement methods so responders hunt and eradicate all attacker footholds, not just the initial alert
questions.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK gives responders a structured catalog of TTPs so when one technique is found, they know which associated persistence, credential-access, and lateral movement techniques to check and eradicate.

questions.question: Which NTFS file system structures are commonly analyzed during disk forensics to trace file metadata and file system change journals?
options: Master File Table ($MFT), $LogFile, and $UsnJrnl
nmap-service-probes and nmap-os-db
Syslog Facility 4 and PRIVAL headers
WinPmem and LiME kernel modules
questions.answer: Master File Table ($MFT), $LogFile, and $UsnJrnl
questions.explanation: Disk forensics analyzes the NTFS Master File Table ($MFT), transaction logs ($LogFile), and update sequence number journal ($UsnJrnl) alongside web history and deleted file remnants.

questions.question: In NIST SP 800-61 Phase 3, what is the purpose of Long-Term Containment compared to Short-Term Containment?
options: Applying temporary fixes (such as emergency patches or clean temporary infrastructure) so business operations can continue safely while forensic evidence is preserved
Permanently wiping all corporate hard drives before detection begins
Publishing the incident root cause to external media
Running an initial ICMP ping sweep on the guest Wi-Fi
questions.answer: Applying temporary fixes (such as emergency patches or clean temporary infrastructure) so business operations can continue safely while forensic evidence is preserved
questions.explanation: Long-term containment keeps business processes running securely using temporary infrastructure or emergency patches until full eradication and clean recovery can be completed.

questions.question: In Step 3.2 of the Week 8 lab, what is the purpose of running `sudo nmap -p 80 --script=http-enum,http-title 192.168.56.20`?
options: To identify hidden web directories, administrative portals, page titles, and server header metadata
To test anonymous FTP login and vsftpd backdoor triggers
To check for MS17-010 EternalBlue on SMB shares
To dump physical RAM from the Apache web server
questions.answer: To identify hidden web directories, administrative portals, page titles, and server header metadata
questions.explanation: `http-enum` enumerates common web directories and admin panels, while `http-title` retrieves the web page title and server metadata.

questions.question: In the Week 8 lab topology, what are the roles and sample IP addresses of the two VMs, and why must scans be restricted to the isolated subnet?
options: Attacker VM (Kali Linux, 192.168.56.10) scans Victim VM (Metasploitable2, 192.168.56.20); unauthorized active scanning of public/external targets is illegal and violates acceptable use policies
Attacker VM (Windows 11, 8.8.8.8) scans Victim VM (Router, 1.1.1.1); scanning public targets is encouraged for practice
Attacker VM (Metasploitable2, 192.168.56.20) scans Victim VM (Kali Linux, 192.168.56.10); scanning is only illegal on Tuesdays
Both VMs share IP 127.0.0.1 and bridge directly to the internet
questions.answer: Attacker VM (Kali Linux, 192.168.56.10) scans Victim VM (Metasploitable2, 192.168.56.20); unauthorized active scanning of public/external targets is illegal and violates acceptable use policies
questions.explanation: The lab explicitly warns that active port scanning against unauthorized networks or public internet targets is illegal; all scans must target only the isolated Victim VM (192.168.56.20) from the Attacker VM (192.168.56.10).
